source_evaluation.decision: Used planetsig/ufo-reports as the sole corpus (source 1 in the brief was unreachable without credentials; this is exactly the source named as the fallback alternative in the brief, source 2).

source.name: planetsig/ufo-reports (GitHub user Sigmond Axel)
source.underlying_data: National UFO Reporting Center (NUFORC), www.nuforc.org public sighting reports. This community conversion project scraped, cleaned, and geocoded the NUFORC archive; it is not an official NUFORC data product. NUFORC's own terms of service prohibit scraping/redistribution of their raw site content, a fact this dataset's own authors (and the alternative timothyrenner/nuforc_sightings_data repo) explicitly acknowledge; this file has nonetheless circulated openly and been mirrored/re-published on GitHub, Kaggle, and data.world for over a decade and is the most commonly cited 'NUFORC CSV' in public UFO-data analyses.
source.geocoding_method: City/place-name level geocoding against opengeocode.org, MaxMind worldcities.csv / us-citylatlng.csv / us-state-countylatlng.csv, with remaining unmatched place names run through findlatitudelongitude.com in batch mode. This means coordinates resolve to a city/place centroid, NOT the precise witness location -- multiple sightings in the same city on different dates will share identical lat/lon.

vintage.note: A handful of pre-1945 sightings (13 rows total across 1906-1944) are retrospective reports -- witnesses recalling and submitting decades-old events -- not contemporaneous records; this is normal for civilian UFO-reporting archives and is not evidence of a data error. Volume is negligible (1990s: 9,214 kept rows; 2000s: 38,782; 2010-2014: 26,044) confirming the corpus is dominated by the post-1990s NUFORC online reporting era, consistent with NUFORC launching web-based report submission in the mid-1990s.
vintage.cutoff: Data collection stops mid-2014 (last full month present is a partial 2014 -- only 2 kept records dated 2014 -- reflecting the file's 2014-06-30 consolidation timestamp). This corpus does NOT include any NUFORC reports from mid-2014 to present (over a decade of subsequent reports, which NUFORC's live database continues to accumulate, are absent from this file).

counts.note_on_bad_coordinates: Exactly one row failed float parsing: a 1974 Mescalero Indian Reservation, NM sighting with latitude field '33q.200088' (a stray letter 'q' before the decimal, almost certainly a data-entry/OCR-style typo for '33.200088', which is the correct latitude for that location). Per this project's no-fabrication rule the row was dropped rather than silently corrected.

dedup.rule: Exact match on (datetime string, latitude string, longitude string) as instructed. Because this corpus geocodes to city-level centroids, groups with >1 row genuinely represent multiple independent NUFORC report submissions describing what is very likely the same sighting event witnessed from the same city at the same timestamp (e.g. a mass sighting reported separately by several people) -- collapsing them to one point per instructions, but the collapsed count is preserved as the record's `v` (weight) field rather than discarded, consistent with this repo's existing convention (loss-crashes.json uses `v` for multi-fatality weight at a single coordinate).

us_vs_non_us.method: Same rough rectangular bounding-box heuristic already used by power-datacenters.provenance.json in this repo (continental US + AK + HI boxes; not a real border polygon). Chosen over trusting the CSV's own `country` field because that field is blank for 9,670 of 80,332 raw rows (~12%) -- mostly US state-only entries that a downstream import evidently failed to backfill with 'us' -- so a naive count on the country column alone would understate the US share.
us_vs_non_us.caveat: The bbox is rectangular, not a real national border; a small number of points near the US/Canada or US/Mexico border could be misclassified. Also note northern Mexico and the Canadian border strip could clip into the continental box slightly -- this is the same acknowledged limitation as the existing power-datacenters layer in this repo.

hotspot_plausibility_check.method: Spot-checked whether well-known NUFORC hotspots show up dense in the kept records, as a sanity check that geocoding/dedup did not silently corrupt the corpus, against a low-population control region of similar box size.

checks.finding: 51 kept records dated exactly 1997 cluster tightly within a few hundredths of a degree of Phoenix, with shapes 'triangle', 'formation', 'chevron', 'sphere' -- an unmistakable match to the well-documented 'Phoenix Lights' mass sighting of March 13, 1997. Confirms geocoding and dedup preserved the real event signature rather than corrupting or over-collapsing it.

checks.area: Pacific Northwest (WA/OR bbox, lat 42-49, lon -125 to -117)
checks.finding: Dense as expected for a widely-cited NUFORC hotspot region.

checks.area: Wyoming control (similar-size bbox, lat 41-45, lon -111 to -104; lowest-population US state, no particular UFO-lore reputation)
checks.finding: An order of magnitude sparser than Phoenix's box despite a comparable box area, consistent with density tracking population/reporting propensity rather than being uniform noise.

checks.area: Outlier check: one kept record at (-82.863, -135.0), 1994, shape 'fireball'
checks.finding: Initially looked like a bad coordinate (open ocean near Antarctica). Traced back to the raw source row: city field literally reads 'antarctica (ross ice shelf) (antarctica)', country blank. A genuine self-reported sighting from an Antarctic expedition/station, correctly geocoded to a remote real-world location -- not a data defect. Left in the corpus as a legitimate non-US record.

caveats: Reporting bias, not sighting bias: this is a self-reported civilian archive, not a verified catalog of aerial phenomena. Density reflects population, cultural predisposition to report, and regional NUFORC awareness at least as much as any actual rate of anomalous sightings -- e.g. dense California/Pacific-Northwest/Florida/Texas clusters track major population centers, not necessarily 'true' hotspots.

Corpus vintage: consolidated 2014-06-30 and not updated since (source repo's last commit touching the data files was 2014-07-08). NUFORC's live database has continued to grow for over a decade past this snapshot; none of that later data is represented here.

City-level geocoding, not report-level: coordinates are the geocoded city/place centroid, not the witness's precise location. Many sightings in the same town land on the exact same point; this is expected and is the reason the dedup step exists, not a sign of duplicate scraping.

'Shape' and free-text fields are self-reported and unverified; 'light', 'triangle', 'circle' dominate simply because those are the easiest shapes to describe from a distant, brief observation at night -- not evidence about the physical nature of anything observed.

This is explicitly a community-maintained, unofficial conversion of NUFORC's public site content. NUFORC's terms of service prohibit scraping and redistribution of their data; this file has nonetheless been circulating openly (GitHub, Kaggle, data.world mirrors) for over a decade. It is used here, unmodified in substance, as the largest reachable geocoded NUFORC-derived corpus per the task brief -- flagged for downstream awareness, not hidden.

A small number of pre-1990 rows (139 kept records across the 1940s-1980s) are almost certainly retrospective/recalled reports rather than contemporaneous ones; treat the pre-1990 tail as thin and less reliable than the 1990s-2014 bulk of the corpus.
One row was dropped for an unparseable coordinate (data-entry typo, not a systemic issue) -- see counts.note_on_bad_coordinates.
